title: Braud's life story: birth, early bands, bass, Kid Ory and Alcorn
summary: In one long answer Braud gives his birth in 1891, early drums and violin, the Olympia band in Chicago, bass influences, a year with Kid Ory and the Creole band.

story.theme_name: Stating your name and birth date on tape
story.community_name: Opening the tape: name, birth date and birthplace

blocks.x: January the 25th. Was there a particular time? Was it in the country? In the country, yeah. I fought on the rice farm there. Still on it. And I came up on the rice farm. And I was a man who played the violins at the end of eight years. I was bringing my music for it when I was eager to work. And I started playing professional around New Orleans, ballrooms, and parks, street parades, drums. And I played with a little brass band around a place called Jamestown in Louisiana, what they call the Beehive Brass Band. And I played a few engagements on drums with Professor Claiborne William of Donnisonville, St. Joseph Band at that time. Then I played around New Orleans up until about around 1940. Then I left Chicago, Illinois. And in Chicago, Illinois, I joined the original three-hole band. That was called the Olympia Band in New Orleans. George Backlade, Freddie Keppert, Roy Palmer, Tubby Hall, and myself on the bass. I studied bass based on Professor Jackson in Chicago. Then I studied trombone in the meantime because that was always my favorite instrument. And my inspiration in the trombone were kid-roy. So I copied that style fully good. And the boys used to call me young-roy around Chicago. So around 1990, my lips went bad. So I just stuck to the spring bass and I made better success out of it. And everyone thought that I did such a wonderful job. And in my bass career, I always admired William Moran and Kimberl, New Orleans. A very fine bass player at that time. So I copied what they were putting down in the line of tone. And fingering, you see the bass violin is a chord instrument, like any other instrument that's supposed to be called. But going back to the bass players of the day, well, I can see a fellow like Milton Hilt, who's very, very fine artist. Slam still, very fine. Jimmy Blanton, one of the greatest solos of all time. And the average bass player, though, they play more like they play in the drum. They play on one string all night. Four in the bow and everything. Never a chord. So I can tell you that a bass is a very fine instrument that's playing right. And I still like to play the bass. And I think I can do a very good job on the bass today. Perhaps I might not be as fast as I used to be, but I don't know. All I have to do is be around somebody that can play because I'm very sensitive about playing. As long as I'm with a band out that can play, I can play. And I really, I had a year with Kidd over his band and I really enjoyed it because he's one fellow that I always liked his playing, who liked to play in his band, always admired him. And so I had the opportunity of playing here in Gabriel. And that was to the height of my ambition. And I really enjoyed it. And I made quite a few platters with him. And I think it was very good. And in the meantime, he had been recording under a company they called the Good Time Jazz, Los Angeles. And for the last six or seven years, he was contracted with them. But Mr. Les of the Good Time Jazz Recording, the manager, he said he think the records that I produced in that story was the best record he ever made since he was recording for the company. And I thought that was very good myself. And I also liked some dates that he made after Calvin Alcon, close to Walker B. And Maple Leaf Rag, I thought that was very, very fun. So then dates I can tell you that I really enjoyed from all of it. Now I was with Alga's Creole Band in 1919. Alga is also from New Orleans. He was a leader. He had a 17-piece band at the Minnesota Pier in Chicago, Illinois.
